title: Loops
description: Learn C# loop constructs including for, foreach, while, and do-while. Understand loop anatomy, control flow statements like break and continue, nested loops, and when to choose each loop type for different scenarios.

data.text: Computers excel at repetition. A loop is a control structure that allows a block of code to execute repeatedly while or until a specified condition is met. Without loops, you would have to write the same line of code hundreds or thousands of times manually. Loops eliminate that tedium and make programs scalable and efficient.
What Are Loops

At their core, all loops answer one question: 'Should I run this code block again?' Each iteration of a loop is one full execution of its body. Most loops have three essential parts: an initialization step that sets up a starting value, a condition that determines whether to continue looping, and an update step that changes state for the next iteration.

data.caption: The repeated decision cycle that powers every loop
data.definition:
flowchart TD
    Start([Loop starts]) --> Init[Initialize counter/variable]
    Init --> Check{Condition met?}
    Check -- Yes --> Run[Execute loop body]
    Run --> Update[Update counter/variable]
    Update --> Check
    Check -- No --> End([Loop ends])

data.text: The for Loop

The for loop is the go-to choice when you know how many times you want to repeat something. It is especially useful when you are counting from one number to another. The for statement contains three expressions separated by semicolons: initialization, condition, and iterator. All three are optional, but omitting the condition creates an infinite loop.

The initialization runs once at the very beginning. The condition is checked before every iteration — if false, the loop stops. The iterator runs after every iteration, typically incrementing or decrementing the counter. You can declare multiple variables in the initialization and apply multiple updates in the iterator, though this should be done sparingly for readability.

data.text: The foreach Loop

The foreach loop is designed specifically for iterating over collections — arrays, lists, strings, and any type that implements IEnumerable. It is the safest and most readable loop when you only need to read each element. The loop variable is read-only inside a foreach; you cannot modify the collection while iterating.

foreach eliminates the risk of off-by-one errors because it automatically stops when the collection ends. You never need to manage an index manually. If you need the index position alongside each element, you can use a regular for loop or the LINQ extension method Select with its index overload.

Modifying a Collection During foreach
data.text: Throwing an exception at runtime, modifying the collection (add/remove) while inside a foreach loop. Use a regular for loop or collect changes and apply them afterward.
The while Loop

The while loop is the simplest loop structure. It has only one part: a condition. The condition is evaluated before every iteration. If it is true, the body runs. If it is false, the loop terminates immediately. Because the condition is checked first, a while loop may execute zero times if the condition is false from the start.

Use while when you do not know how many iterations you need in advance. For example, reading lines from a file until the end, or waiting for a user to enter valid input. The loop keeps going until some external condition changes.

data.text: The do-while Loop

The do-while loop is almost identical to while, with one critical difference: the condition is checked after the body runs, not before. This guarantees the body executes at least once, even if the condition is initially false. This makes do-while ideal for menu systems, confirmation prompts, and any scenario where you want the user to see options before deciding whether to continue.

Counter variable scoped to the loop

cards.title: foreach
cards.description: Best for reading every element in a collection. The compiler handles the iteration logic.

cards.title: while
cards.description: Best when the number of iterations is unknown. Condition is checked before each run.

cards.title: do-while
cards.description: Like while but guarantees at least one execution. Condition is checked after the body.
pros: Body always runs at least once
cons: Same infinite loop risk as while

data.text: break and continue

Sometimes you need to alter a loop's normal flow before its condition becomes false. The break statement immediately terminates the nearest enclosing loop and transfers control to the first statement after it. The continue statement is more subtle: it skips the rest of the current iteration and jumps directly to the next condition evaluation.

A common pattern is to use break when you have found what you are looking for, avoiding unnecessary iterations. Use continue when you want to skip specific items but keep processing the rest of the collection.

data.title: Infinite Loops
data.text: A loop whose condition never becomes false will run forever. This freezes the application. Common causes: forgetting to increment the counter, using assignment (=) instead of comparison (==) in the condition, or a logic error that always evaluates to true. Always ensure your loop has a clear exit path.
Nested Loops

A loop placed inside another loop is called a nested loop. For each single iteration of the outer loop, the inner loop completes all of its iterations. Nested loops are powerful for working with multi-dimensional data like grids, matrices, or tables. However, they multiply execution time: an outer loop of 10 with an inner loop of 10 runs 100 iterations total. Be mindful of performance with deeply nested loops over large datasets.

data.text: Loop Performance Considerations

data.title: Tips for writing efficient loops
items: Avoid heavy computations inside the loop condition — compute them once before the loop
Use foreach instead of for when you do not need the index — it is optimized for readability
Break early when you have found what you need instead of iterating the entire collection
Cache collection lengths outside the loop condition in for loops with large arrays
Avoid nested loops over large datasets — consider LINQ or hash-based lookups instead

data.description: Write a method called IsPrime that accepts an integer and returns a boolean. Use a for loop to check divisibility from 2 up to the square root of the number. Return false immediately if any divisor is found (use break). Add input validation for numbers less than 2.

items.question: Can I use break in a foreach loop?
items.answer: Yes. break works in all loop types in C# including foreach, for, while, and do-while. It immediately exits the nearest enclosing loop regardless of the loop type.

items.question: Is foreach slower than for?
items.answer: For arrays, the performance difference is negligible. For List<T>, foreach may be slightly slower in older .NET versions, but modern runtimes optimize it heavily. Always prioritize readability unless profiling shows a real bottleneck.

items.question: Why would I use do-while instead of while?
items.answer: Use do-while when you need the loop body to execute at least once. A common example is prompting the user for input — you always need to show the prompt at least once before checking whether to repeat.

items.question: Can I nest a foreach inside a for loop?
items.answer: Yes. You can nest any loop type inside any other loop type. Just be aware that nested loops multiply the total iterations. A 10-iteration outer loop with a 10-iteration inner loop performs 100 total iterations.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: for loops are best when you know how many iterations you need
foreach loops are safest for reading collection elements
while loops handle unknown iteration counts with pre-condition checks
do-while guarantees at least one execution with post-condition checks
break exits a loop immediately; continue skips to the next iteration
Infinite loops occur when the exit condition is never reached
Nested loops process multi-dimensional data but multiply iteration count
data.takeaway: Loops let your program repeat work efficiently. Choosing the right loop type for each situation makes your code clearer, safer, and easier to debug.
